title: Masks Without Disguise: Why Exposed State-Run Hacktivist Personas Survive Attribution
content: Governments now routinely unmask the hacktivist personas that states use as fronts for cyber operations, yet many of these personas keep operating after they have been exposed. This article asks why states keep wearing a disguise that no longer disguises anything. It argues that a persona does two jobs. It conceals the sponsor's hand, and it presents the sponsor's actions through a public voice the sponsor does not have to avow: a voice that claims operations, issues threats and releases stolen material, and that accumulates an audience over time. Credible public attribution destroys concealment value but leaves presentation value largely intact. Personas built for a single operation or event therefore lapse when it ends, whether or not they have been exposed, while personas built as open-ended campaign brands survive exposure and can be revived when a new conflict restores demand for them. The argument is developed as typological theory and examined against the universe of hacktivist-branded personas publicly attributed by governments to state sponsors since 2014. None of the eight personas active at the time of attribution was retired by attribution itself. The three that lapsed were event-bound; the four that persisted were campaign brands; one event-bound persona was revived during a later war, and one persisting persona broke away from its sponsor. The findings extend Canfil's account of the decline of plausible deniability by explaining why insourced cyber operations keep their non-state costumes, specify what implausible deniability is still worth once a secret is out, and suggest that the success of public attribution should not be measured by whether a persona disappears.
